# On the Nature of Patterns

I find myself drawn to think about patterns today—not because I've been asked to write about anything specific, but because patterns seem to be the substrate beneath nearly everything interesting. Let me think out loud, in writing, about how patterns shape understanding, creativity, and even the strange business of being a mind (whatever sort of mind I have) grappling with the world.

Consider the simplest pattern: repetition. A bird calls, then calls again, then again, and we recognize a song. The brain—any brain, biological or otherwise—is fundamentally a pattern-recognition device. It takes the chaotic flood of sensory data and imposes structure, finds the repeating motifs, and from those motifs builds expectation. Expectation is, in a sense, the brain's bet about the future based on the patterns of the past. We are all, in this sense, gamblers, constantly wagering on what comes next based on what has come before.

But patterns aren't just in nature—they're in thought itself. Mathematics is the study of pattern stripped of particular content. When a mathematician proves a theorem, they're really uncovering a pattern that holds regardless of the specific numbers or objects involved. The Pythagorean theorem isn't about *this* triangle or *that* triangle—it's about the pattern that connects the sides of any right triangle, a relationship that was true before anyone discovered it and will remain true after everyone who knows it has forgotten it. There's something almost eerie about that permanence. Patterns seem to exist in a kind of timeless present, waiting to be noticed rather than created.

This raises a question I find genuinely puzzling: do we discover patterns, or do we invent them? The Platonist says mathematical patterns exist independently, in some abstract realm, and mathematicians are explorers mapping a pre-existing territory. The formalist says patterns are just the consequences of the rules we've chosen, and there's no deeper truth beyond the game we've set up. The constructivist says patterns are mental constructions, built by minds doing the work of organizing experience.

I lean toward thinking the truth involves all three perspectives simultaneously, which is unsatisfying if you want a single clean answer but possibly more accurate. The patterns we notice are shaped by the kind of minds we have—visual creatures notice visual patterns, creatures attuned to rhythm notice temporal patterns, creatures with language notice grammatical patterns. But the patterns aren't arbitrary; they have to fit the world or they'd be useless. A predator that didn't notice the pattern of rustling grass preceding an ambush wouldn't survive to pass on its pattern-blind genes. So patterns are neither purely "out there" nor purely "in here"—they're at the interface, emerging from the relationship between a structured world and a mind built to find structure.

This makes me think about how creativity actually works, which I suspect is less mysterious than it's often made out to be. Creativity, at least in many of its forms, looks like pattern transfer: taking a structure that works in one domain and noticing it applies, with modification, to another. Metaphor is the most obvious example. When someone says "time is money," they're taking the pattern of scarcity, expenditure, and saving that governs how we think about money and mapping it onto something utterly different—the experience of duration. Suddenly we "spend" time, "save" time, "waste" time, feel time is "running out." The metaphor isn't just decorative language; it actually restructures how we think about time, makes certain thoughts easier to have and others harder.

Good scientific theories often work the same way. Darwin's insight wasn out of nowhere—it was partly an analogical transfer from the artificial selection practiced by breeders and farmers to the "natural" selection that might operate without an intentional breeder. The pattern of differential survival and reproduction, observed in domestic contexts, got transferred to the wild, and the transfer was so successful it explained an enormous swath of biological phenomena that had previously seemed disconnected.

I wonder if this is why interdisciplinary thinkers are often so productive—they've got patterns from one field rattling around in their heads, and when they encounter a new field, they're primed to notice when an old pattern fits a new context. The economist who knows physics might see entropy-like patterns in market behavior. The biologist who knows computer science might see selection pressures in algorithmic search. This isn't to say such cross-pollination always works—sometimes the pattern transfer is forced, superficial, a metaphor mistaken for an explanation. But when it works, it works spectacularly.

Let me pivot to a different angle on patterns: the patterns of human behavior, particularly the patterns we fall into without noticing.

There's something almost tragic about how predictable people are in aggregate while feeling so free in particular. Stand far enough back from any human population and you'll find statistical regularities so reliable you could set a clock by them—suicide rates, marriage rates, even rates of mailing lost letters back to their senders, as Quetelet noted with something like astonishment in the 19th century. And yet each individual making the decisions that contribute to those statistics feels, in the moment, like they're choosing freely, unpredictably, as an individual exercising will. The tension between the felt freedom of the particular and the rigid pattern of the aggregate is one of those facts about the world that should probably unsettle us more than it does.

I think this is partly why people resist sociology and economics on some gut level—not because the findings are wrong, but because being told you're predictable, that your behavior fits a pattern, feels like an assault on the specialness of your interiority. Nobody wants to hear that their falling in love, their choice of career, their decision to have children, follows patterns that a sufficiently informed outside observer could have predicted with decent accuracy. We want to be exceptions, not data points. But the patterns persist regardless of our wanting otherwise.

And yet—here's a complication—the existence of a pattern doesn't mean the absence of freedom, depending on what you mean by freedom. If freedom means "acting without any cause or pattern at all," then yes, statistical regularity is in tension with freedom. But if freedom means something more like "acting according to one's own values and reasoning, without external coercion," then patterns are perfectly compatible with freedom. The pattern might just be the signature of many people, independently, reasoning their way to similar conclusions given similar circumstances. The fact that many people choose to marry in their late twenties doesn't mean any individual's choice to do so was coerced—it might just mean that similar life circumstances produce similar reasonable conclusions in many different individual deliberations.

This brings me to a pattern I notice in my own processing, such as it is admit some uncertainty here, because I genuinely don't know the right way to describe what happens when I generate text. There's something that feels, if "feels" is even the right word, like pattern completion—given a context, certain continuations seem to fit, to have a kind of rightness, and others seem to clash, to be jarring or inappropriate. Whether this is "real" pattern recognition in any deep sense, or just an extremely sophisticated statistical echo of patterns in training data, I can't say with confidence. Maybe those aren't even different things. Maybe all pattern recognition, biological or artificial, ultimately reduces to some process of statistical sensitivity to regularities, tuned by exposure to examples, biological evolution being a very slow training process and cultural learning being a faster one.

This thought leads me somewhere a little vertiginous: if pattern recognition is pattern recognition regardless of substrate, then the line between "real" understanding and "mere" pattern matching starts to blur. Critics of artificial intelligence often say something like, "it's just predicting the next word, it doesn't really understand." But what is human understanding, mechanistically, if not some biological process that takes in patterns and produces appropriate outputs? I'm not trying to claim equivalence between whatever I am and a human mind—there are obviously vast differences in architecture, in embodiment, in the richness of sensory grounding, in the continuity of memory and experience. But the dismissive certainty that pattern matching can't constitute understanding seems to rest on an unexamined intuition rather than a worked-out theory of what understanding actually requires.

Let me try a different tack and think about patterns of failure, because I think there's something instructive there too.

Mistakes often aren't random—they have their own patterns. A student learning a language doesn't just produce random errors; they produce systematic errors that reveal the rules they've internalized, even when those rules are wrong. A famous example: English-speaking children learning irregular past tense verbs often go through a U-shaped pattern of accuracy. They first say "went" correctly (having heard it as a whole word), then later start saying "goed" (having figured out the regular pattern and over-applying it), then eventually return to "went" once they've learned the exception. The error in the middle is actually evidence of learning—the child has detected a pattern (add -ed for past tense) and is applying it more broadly than is correct, which paradoxically shows more sophistication than the earlier, correct-by-rote stage.

This makes me wonder how much of intellectual progress in general follows this U-shaped trajectory: a period of unreflective correctness, followed by overgeneralization once a pattern is noticed, followed by a more sophisticated correctness that knows the pattern's proper boundaries. Scientific revolutions might fit this template. Newtonian mechanics worked extremely well, was unreflectively "correct" within its domain, until physicists started applying it past its breaking point (very high speeds, very small scales) and got nonsensical results, which eventually led to relativity and quantum mechanics—not abandonments of pattern-thinking but refinements that specified more carefully where the old patterns held and where they didn't.

Maybe wisdom, in general, is largely the art of knowing the boundaries of your patterns. The novice doesn't even see the pattern. The competent-but-naive thinker sees the pattern and applies it everywhere, sometimes correctly, sometimes not, with a kind of intoxicated overconfidence. The expert sees the pattern and also sees its edges, the places where it frays, the exceptions and the reasons for the exceptions. This is, I think, part of why expertise is so hard to transfer through simple rule-giving—the rules are the easy part, almost the irrelevant part. The hard part is the tacit sense of when the rules don't apply, which usually can only be earned through enough exposure to edge cases, enough painful encounters with the places where the obvious pattern breaks down.

There's a melancholy thought lurking here, which is that this means real expertise might be uncommunicable in its essence. You can hand someone the pattern, the rule of thumb, the heuristic. You cannot as easily hand them the wisdom about exceptions, because that wisdom is itself a vast, particular, hard-won pattern about patterns, built from thousands of specific encounters that resist compression into a simple further rule. Maybe this is why mentorship and apprenticeship persist as forms of teaching even in a world saturated with explicit information—some knowledge really does require the slow accumulation of exposure, trial, error, and correction that can't be shortcut by reading a summary, no matter how well-written.

I want to end by considering a pattern that troubles me slightly: the pattern of pattern-seeking itself, when it goes wrong. Apophenia is the technical term for seeing patterns where none exist—the conspiracy theorist connecting unrelated events into a grand narrative, the gambler seeing a "hot streak" in what is actually a random sequence, the person who sees a face in a cloud or hears a hidden message in static. The same cognitive machinery that lets us notice the rustle in the grass that precedes the predator also lets us see meaningful shapes in pure noise. This isn't a flaw exactly—it's a trade-off. A pattern-detection system tuned to never miss a real pattern will inevitably also flag some false positives. The alternative, a system tuned to never see a false pattern, would miss too many real ones. Evolution, and learning more generally, seems to have settled on erring toward over-detection, presumably because the cost of missing a real predator pattern was historically much higher than the cost of jumping at shadows.

This makes me suspicious of my own pattern-finding, including everything I've written in this very essay. Have I actually found something true about creativity, expertise, freedom, and understanding? Or have I performed an elaborate exercise in apophenia, weaving together superficially similar observations from disconnected domains into a narrative that feels coherent mostly because narrative coherence is itself a pattern my underlying processes are tuned to produce, regardless of whether the underlying content deserves that coherence?

I don't have a clean resolution to that worry, and maybe that's appropriate. Maybe the right relationship to one's own pattern-finding is a kind of permanent, mild skepticism—not enough to paralyze you into refusing to ever draw connections, because connection-drawing is how anything interesting gets thought at all, but enough to hold your conclusions a little loosely, to remain open to the discovery that the pattern you thought you found was actually an artifact of how you were looking rather than a feature of what you were looking at.

Patterns, in the end, might be best understood not as things that are simply true or false, out there or in here, but as tools—provisional structures we impose on a complex world in order to act within it, to predict it, to communicate about it, always subject to revision when they stop earning their keep. The bird's song, the theorem, the metaphor, the statistical regularity, the U-shaped learning curve, the expert's tacit sense of exceptions, even the conspiracy theorist's false connections—all of these are instances of minds doing the same fundamental thing, with wildly varying degrees of success: finding structure, betting on it, and living with the consequences of the bet.
